# Memory and State

::: {.callout-question}

What should the system remember, and how does it recall it?

:::

The child teaches the robot her name, and that she likes the blue cup, and that
the lamp goes off at eight. The next day it remembers. That is the moment the
robot stops being a demo and starts being hers, and it is also the moment it
starts keeping a record of a child's life.

Both halves matter. Memory is what makes the system feel like it has a history.
It is also a liability that grows every day it runs. So the question is not whether to remember. It is what to keep,
in what form, and what to forget.

## Memory is a budget and a liability

Persistence is two things at once: a component you build and a property you are
judged on. As a component it is storage and a recall path. As a property it
trades against privacy, because everything kept about a private space is a record
that can leak, and against storage and recall latency, because state that only
grows eventually does not fit and is slow to search.

::: {.column-margin}
**Properties in tension**: memory and state against privacy, under a storage and
recall-latency budget.
:::

Keep everything and all three turn against you. Storage fills. Recall slows as
the system searches a larger pile each time. And the record of the room grows
without bound, which is the privacy budget going quietly into deficit. The only
way out is to forget on purpose, which makes the design question sharp: what is
worth keeping?

## The state grows unless you forget

The arithmetic is unforgiving. State is just what you keep, summed:

$$\text{state} = (\text{memories kept}) \times (\text{bytes per memory}) \le \text{storage}$$

Memories arrive at some rate for as long as the robot is awake, so without a
forgetting policy the left side climbs until it hits the limit, and recall
latency climbs with it. A forgetting policy is therefore not housekeeping; it is
the mechanism that keeps memory inside its budget. The decision the chapter asks
of you is the policy itself: which memories earn their bytes, and which are
dropped or summarized once their value has decayed. For the small facts a robot
keeps, raw storage is rarely what binds; recall latency and the privacy surface
both grow with the state long before the disk fills, and those are the limits the
forgetting policy actually answers to.

## What to keep, and in what form

The harder half of the decision is the form. @fig-structured-memory shows the
choice. Structured memory keeps facts as nodes and relations you can read: the
child is called a name, likes blue, owns a rabbit. You can see exactly what the
system knows, because you put it there, and you can delete one fact on its own
when asked. An unstructured store, the dense vector index behind most retrieval
systems, recalls by similarity, which is powerful but soft. It has no exact,
enumerable list of what it knows: a fact about bedtime may be spread across many
entries and surfaced only by resemblance, so "forget everything about bedtime"
becomes a fuzzy search with no guarantee you found it all. A structured store is
the opposite: every fact is an explicit relation you can list for a parent and
delete by name, certain that what you removed is gone and what remains is all
there is.

::: {#fig-structured-memory fig-cap="**Structured memory is enumerable**: each fact is an explicit node you can list and delete by name, so forgetting one thing is exact; a similarity-based vector store offers no such enumerable, auditable list." fig-alt="A small knowledge graph. A central node labeled child connects by labeled edges to four fact nodes: a name, likes blue, owns a toy rabbit, and a routine bedtime. The bedtime node is dashed and labeled forget on request, showing one fact can be removed on its own."}
![](../assets/diagrams/structured-memory.svg)
:::

For a robot in a child's room the binding property is privacy, and privacy favors
the form you can audit and prune, the promise a similarity index cannot keep.
Recall quality may argue the other way for some tasks,
and the honest answer is often a small structured core for what must be
inspectable, with vector recall for the rest. The point is that the form is a
privacy decision, not only a retrieval one. One cost the form hides: turning raw
experience into clean facts is itself a parsing-and-resolution step, a
deliberation-loop expense rather than a free local write, and that extraction is
its own small placement decision.

## Build

::: {.callout-build title="Teach it, then make it forget"}

Stand up a small structured memory on the device, a handful of nodes and edges.
Teach it three or four facts the way the child would, and have it recall them in a
later session. Then replay a simulated week of interactions in a few minutes and
measure two things across it: recall accuracy, and how the state grows per
interaction.

Then test the other direction. Ask it to forget one fact and confirm that exactly
that fact is gone and the rest survives. Finally, account for the privacy cost:
if you moved this memory to a server for better recall, write down precisely what
bytes about the child would leave the device. That number is the privacy budget,
made concrete.

If you cannot run the full loop, use the provided graph and recall log and make
the keep-or-forget calls on paper.

:::

## What the number says

State growth is rarely linear in practice, because the interesting memories
cluster: a burst when the robot is new, then a slow trickle. Recall accuracy
usually holds for the structured core and decays for anything you let drift into a
vague store. The reconciliation is to see that the cheap win is not a bigger
index. It is a sharper forgetting policy, which keeps the state small, the recall
fast, and the privacy surface narrow, all at once.

## Read

The contrast in this chapter is structured knowledge representation against
retrieval-augmented generation (Lewis et al., 2020), which is the dense-vector
recall the structured store is weighed against. The forgetting question is the
data-minimization principle from privacy practice: keep the least you can, and be
able to delete on request. The engineering and the ethics point the same way
here, toward keeping less and keeping it legible.

::: {.callout-teaching}

- **Hook**: show the graph growing as the child teaches the robot, then say "here
  is everything it knows, and you put it there." The inspectability is the lesson
  before any retrieval mechanism is named.
- **Open question**: episodic versus semantic memory, one chapter or two? For now
  the structured core carries both; split only if the recall mechanisms diverge
  enough to need separate treatment.
- **Watch**: keep privacy in the foreground. It is tempting to make this a pure
  retrieval-quality chapter; the reason the form matters here is that the room is
  a child's.

:::
